title: Precedent and the Art of Distinction
text:
Judicial reasoning in common-law systems rests heavily on precedent, the principle that courts should follow earlier decisions on materially similar facts. Yet precedent is rarely applied mechanically, because every case presents a constellation of facts that can be characterised in competing ways. A skilled advocate therefore seeks to distinguish an unfavourable ruling by emphasising some detail that the earlier court deemed immaterial. The resulting contest over what counts as the 'ratio decidendi' lies at the heart of legal argument.

Critics of this approach argue that the distinguishing process can become a tool of convenience, allowing judges to reach predetermined outcomes while preserving the appearance of consistency. Defenders reply that this flexibility is essential, since rigid adherence to the letter of earlier judgments would freeze the law and prevent it from responding to changed social circumstances. The tension, in their view, is not a defect but the very mechanism by which law evolves. Whether that evolution is principled or merely opportunistic remains one of the most persistent questions in jurisprudence.

questions.text: According to the first paragraph, what is precedent?
options: The principle that courts should follow earlier decisions on materially similar facts
A statute enacted by the legislature to replace case law
A written agreement between two opposing lawyers
The final appeal available after a trial court's judgment

questions.text: According to the second paragraph, what do critics argue the distinguishing process can become?
options: A rigid rule that prevents any judicial discretion
A method that has been abolished by modern courts
A tool of convenience for reaching predetermined outcomes
A procedure used only by appellate advocates

questions.text: What can be inferred about the author's view of the contest over the 'ratio decidendi'?
options: It is irrelevant once a statute has been enacted
It is central to legal argument and open to strategic manipulation
It is resolved automatically by applying precedent

questions.text: Which position would the defenders of judicial flexibility most likely accept?
options: Rigid adherence to earlier judgments is preferable to any change
Legal change is a natural and necessary result of tension within precedent
Judges should never distinguish a previous ruling
Social circumstances have no bearing on legal reasoning

paragraph_translations: El razonamiento judicial en los sistemas de common law descansa en gran medida en el precedente, el principio según el cual los tribunales deben seguir decisiones anteriores sobre hechos materialmente similares. Sin embargo, el precedente rara vez se aplica de forma mecánica, porque cada caso presenta una constelación de hechos que puede caracterizarse de maneras contrapuestas. Un abogado hábil busca, por ello, distinguir una resolución desfavorable destacando algún detalle que el tribunal anterior consideró irrelevante. La disputa resultante sobre qué cuenta como 'ratio decidendi' se encuentra en el corazón de la argumentación jurídica.

Los críticos de este enfoque sostienen que el proceso de distinción puede convertirse en un instrumento de conveniencia, que permite a los jueces llegar a resultados predeterminados conservando la apariencia de coherencia. Los defensores responden que esta flexibilidad es esencial, pues la adhesión rígida a la letra de las sentencias anteriores congelaría el derecho e impediría que respondiera a circunstancias sociales cambiantes. La tensión, a su juicio, no es un defecto sino el mecanismo mismo mediante el cual el derecho evoluciona. Si esa evolución es fundada en principios o meramente oportunista sigue siendo una de las cuestiones más persistentes de la jurisprudencia.
